case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a motion under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(4) to vacate a default judgment that is void for lack of personal jurisdiction may be denied as untimely under Rule 60(c)(1)’s “reasonable time” requirement (i.e., whether any time limit applies at all).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(4) (void judgments) and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(c)(1) (requiring Rule 60(b) motions be made “within a reasonable time”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void ab initio, and because void judgments are legal nullities, Rule 60(c)(1) should not impose (and cannot permissibly impose) any time limit on a Rule 60(b)(4) motion seeking to set aside such a judgment; the Sixth Circuit erred by treating “reasonable time” as a timeliness bar even where the underlying default judgment is jurisdictionally void.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues the text is straightforward: Rule 60(c)(1) expressly says any motion under Rule 60(b)—including (b)(4)—must be filed within a reasonable time; the Supreme Court has recently reiterated that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to that requirement, and allowing unlimited delay would undermine finality and create serious disruption (here, to a nearly fully administered Chapter 7 estate).
key_precedents: Kemp v. United States (recent Supreme Court statement that all Rule 60(b) motions must be filed within a reasonable time)
United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa, 559 U.S. 260 (2010)
United States for Use & Benefit of Mosher Steel Co. v. Fluor Corp., 436 F.2d 383 (2d Cir. 1970)
Allstate Life Ins. Co. v. Linter Group Ltd., 994 F.2d 996 (2d Cir. 1993)
In re World Trade Ctr. Disaster Site Litig., 722 F.3d 483 (2d Cir. 2013)
Link v. Wabash R.R. Co., 370 U.S. 626 (1962)
United States v. Boch Oldsmobile, Inc., 909 F.2d 657 (1st Cir. 1990)

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument—that a void judgment is a nullity attackable “at any time”—cannot overcome the enacted text of Rule 60(c)(1), which says without qualification that a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made “within a reasonable time.” Justice Alito’s structural point is persuasive: the Rules expressly impose a one-year cap only for (b)(1)–(3), but that does not imply (b)(4) is timeless; it indicates (b)(4) is governed by the separate reasonable-time requirement. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Kemp’s statement that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)(1), together with Espinosa’s admonition (as Justice Sotomayor notes) that (b)(4) is not a license to sleep on rights, supports a narrow, case-specific reasonableness inquiry keyed to notice, diligence, and reliance/finality. That approach preserves prompt relief for truly jurisdictionally void judgments while protecting the system’s interest in finality and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest contention—that a void judgment is a nullity attackable “at any time”—cannot override the enacted text: Rule 60(c)(1) states without qualification that a motion “under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and it contains no (b)(4) carveout. Justice Gorsuch’s structural point reinforces the ordinary textual inference: the Rules expressly exempt only (b)(1)–(3) from the broader “reasonable time” standard by adding a one-year cap, which implies (b)(4) remains governed by that separate reasonableness requirement rather than being wholly untethered from time. Justice Roberts’s reliance on Espinosa further supports reading (b)(4) narrowly and rejecting an atextual “license to sleep on rights,” while still leaving room for prompt relief where notice was lacking. Nothing raised in conference supplies a textual or historically grounded basis to create a categorical timeliness exemption for (b)(4), so I adhere to Respondent.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point—the common-law maxim that a void judgment may be attacked at any time—cannot overcome Rule 60(c)(1)’s enacted, categorical text requiring any motion “under Rule 60(b)” be made within a reasonable time, with no carveout for (b)(4). As Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Kemp’s statement that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c) forecloses the atextual perpetual-attack rule, and Espinosa’s warning (highlighted by the Chief) confirms (b)(4) is narrow and not a license to sleep on rights. Justice Barrett’s point about the Rule’s structure is also decisive: the Rules expressly add a one-year cap only for (b)(1)–(3), which would be unnecessary if (b)(4) already enjoyed an unlimited temporal exemption. A flexible reasonableness inquiry—keyed to notice, diligence, and reliance/finality, especially in bankruptcy—best fits the text and the practical consequences without immunizing true jurisdictional defects from prompt correction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument—that a void judgment is a legal nullity attackable at any time, especially for lack of personal jurisdiction—has real due process force, but it cannot override the Rules’ enacted procedure governing how and when that attack is made. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, Rule 60(c)(1) states without carveout that any motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be brought within a “reasonable time,” and Kemp’s confirmation (noted by Justice Alito) that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to 60(c)(1) makes an atextual perpetual exception for (b)(4) hard to justify. Espinosa’s warning—invoked by the Chief and consistent with my own fairness concerns—that Rule 60(b)(4) is not a license to sleep on rights aligns with a pragmatic approach: once a party has notice, unreasonable delay can inflict serious prejudice on third parties and vulnerable stakeholders who rely on finality, particularly in a substantially administered bankruptcy estate. The “reasonable time” standard remains flexible enough to protect the truly no-notice/no-jurisdiction cases, but it properly prevents strategic or dilatory reopening that would undermine access to justice for others.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains the common-law maxim that a void judgment is a nullity subject to attack “at any time,” but that background principle cannot supply an atextual exemption from Rule 60(c)(1)’s command that a motion “under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time.” Justice Gorsuch’s structural point—that the Rules expressly impose a one-year cap only for (b)(1)–(3) while separately requiring reasonableness for all (b) motions—confirms that (b)(4) is not singled out for perpetual timeliness. Espinosa, as the Chief emphasizes, directly rebuts any notion that (b)(4) is a license to sleep on rights, and Kemp’s statement (noted by several colleagues) that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c) reinforces that we should not create a categorical carveout. A flexible reasonable-time standard can still fully accommodate the hardest due-process cases (e.g., no notice), while protecting reliance interests in settings like a substantially administered bankruptcy estate.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument—that a void judgment is a nullity subject to attack at any time—cannot overcome the enacted text of Rule 60(c)(1), which states categorically that a motion “under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” with no carveout for (b)(4). Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Espinosa is particularly persuasive on this point because it rejects the notion that (b)(4) is “a license for litigants to sleep on their rights,” confirming that voidness does not erase timeliness constraints. Justice Barrett’s discussion of Klapprott is also clarifying: it shows only that the one-year cap for (b)(1)–(3) does not apply to (b)(4), not that (b)(4) escapes the separate reasonable-time requirement applicable to all Rule 60(b) motions. Under a textualist approach, the proper reconciliation is a case-specific “reasonable time” inquiry, not an atextual perpetual exception.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s “void means attackable at any time” maxim has force as a matter of historical practice, especially for personal-jurisdiction defects, but it cannot overcome the enacted text of Rule 60(c)(1), which—without carveout—requires any motion “under Rule 60(b)” to be filed within a reasonable time. Chief Justice Roberts’s focus on the Rule’s unqualified language, together with Justice Alito’s structural point that the Rules expressly impose only a one-year cap for (b)(1)–(3) while still leaving (b)(4) within (c)(1)’s separate reasonable-time constraint, confirms that an atextual categorical exemption would be improper. Justice Gorsuch’s clarification that Klapprott merely shows (b)(4) is not subject to the one-year bar, not that it is timeless, addresses any precedent-based argument for an “any time” rule. Espinosa’s admonition (noted by multiple colleagues) that (b)(4) is not a license to sleep on rights fits an institutionalist concern for finality and reliance—particularly in bankruptcy—while still allowing prompt relief in truly no-notice, no-jurisdiction cases under a context-sensitive reasonableness inquiry.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s “void judgments may be attacked at any time” maxim is a strong background principle, but it cannot override the enacted text of Rule 60(c)(1), which says—without carveout—that a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made “within a reasonable time.” Justice Alito’s structural point is persuasive on a textualist reading: the Rules expressly add a one-year outside limit for (b)(1)–(3), yet still impose the separate reasonable-time requirement on all (b) motions, implying (b)(4) is not exempt from timeliness altogether. Justice Gorsuch’s reminder about Klapprott is also helpful—Klapprott shows only that the one-year cap doesn’t apply to (b)(4), not that (b)(4) escapes Rule 60(c)(1). Espinosa and Kemp further confirm that (b)(4) is narrow and not a license for strategic delay, with reasonableness turning on notice, diligence, and prejudice rather than an atextual perpetual right to reopen.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the traditional maxim that a truly void judgment is a nullity that can be attacked at any time, particularly where personal jurisdiction is absent. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief emphasize, Rule 60(c)(1) is enacted procedural text that applies to any “motion under Rule 60(b),” and it contains no carveout for (b)(4); voidness goes to the merits of the ground for relief, not to whether the movant must act within a reasonable time. Espinosa—highlighted by Justice Sotomayor and Justice Gorsuch—matters for my pragmatic fairness lens because it rejects using (b)(4) as a “license” to sleep on rights once notice exists, especially where reopening would prejudice third parties and destabilize completed proceedings like bankruptcy administration. I therefore remain with Respondent: courts can protect due process while still enforcing a flexible, context-sensitive reasonable-time requirement.

John Roberts.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states without qualification that a motion under Rule 60(b) must be made "within a reasonable time," and the narrowest, most text-faithful reading is that this timeliness requirement applies to (b)(4) as well, with "reasonable" calibrated to the circumstances (including reliance and finality interests). In Espinosa, the Court emphasized that Rule 60(b)(4) relief is reserved for exceptional jurisdictional defects and "does not provide a license for litigants to sleep on their rights," reinforcing that equitable limits remain relevant even when a party labels a judgment "void." That approach preserves institutional legitimacy and the finality of judgments while still allowing relief when a truly void judgment is promptly challenged, particularly important where reopening would disrupt settled proceedings (as in a largely administered bankruptcy estate). This reading aligns with the Court’s recent understanding (e.g., Kemp) that all Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)(1)’s reasonable-time requirement.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Rules’ text controls: Rule 60(c)(1) states that “a motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and nothing in that provision exempts Rule 60(b)(4). The Court has reiterated that all Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)(1)’s timing requirement, and reading in a categorical no-time-limit exception for (b)(4) would contradict the enacted text and undermine finality interests that the Rules were designed to protect. Espinosa confirms that Rule 60(b)(4) is limited to exceptional cases of jurisdictional defect and does not suggest an unlimited, perpetual right to reopen judgments; it instead reinforces that courts may cabin (b)(4) to preserve the stability of final judgments. Accordingly, even assuming the judgment is void for lack of personal jurisdiction, the motion may be denied if not brought within a “reasonable time” under Rule 60(c)(1).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of Rule 60(c)(1) is categorical: "[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time," and it provides an express one-year cap only for (b)(1)–(3), signaling no carve-out for (b)(4) motions. This Court recently reiterated that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)’s deadlines, confirming the straightforward reading that (b)(4) is not exempt. See Kemp v. United States, 596 U.S. at 533; cf. United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa, 559 U.S. 260 (2010) (treating Rule 60(b)(4) relief as limited and consistent with finality concerns). Practical consequences reinforce the textual conclusion: allowing jurisdictional-voidness claims to be raised without any time constraint would undermine finality and disrupt reliance interests, particularly in contexts like a largely administered bankruptcy estate.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states that motions “under Rule 60(b)” must be made “within a reasonable time,” and its plain text applies to (b)(4) as well as other subsections—consistent with this Court’s recent instruction in Kemp v. United States that all Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)(1). Espinosa underscores that Rule 60(b)(4) is not “a license for litigants to sleep on their rights” and recognizes forfeiture principles where a party with notice fails to act, which supports permitting a reasonable-time limit even for voidness claims. A fact-specific “reasonable time” inquiry also better accounts for real-world prejudice to third parties—especially in contexts like a nearly administered Chapter 7 estate—while still allowing robust relief in truly exceptional cases where there was no arguable basis for jurisdiction. Denying any timeliness constraint would invite strategic delay and undermine access to justice for other, more vulnerable stakeholders who rely on finality to obtain distributions and closure.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) says in unqualified terms that “[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and nothing in the text carves out Rule 60(b)(4) motions alleging a jurisdictionally void default judgment. Kemp v. United States reinforces that reading by stating that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the reasonable-time requirement, with only (b)(1)–(3) additionally capped at one year; that statement tracks the rule’s structure and supports enforcing timeliness here. Espinosa also reflects the Court’s reluctance to treat Rule 60(b)(4) as an unconstrained vehicle for belated collateral attacks, emphasizing finality absent a truly fundamental defect. A reasonable-time limit remains workable because it can account for when the movant learned of the judgment and the reliance interests at stake (here, the near-complete administration of a Chapter 7 estate) without rewriting the Rules to create a categorical “any time” exception.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states in mandatory terms that “[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and it creates an express one-year cap only for subsections (b)(1)–(3); the absence of any parallel carveout for (b)(4) is best read as intentional under ordinary textual canons. This Court in Kemp v. United States reiterated that “All” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)’s reasonable-time requirement, and nothing in the Rules’ text authorizes courts to exempt void-judgment motions from that limit. While a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void, the Rules still regulate the timing and manner of seeking relief from final judgments, and reading an atextual “no time limit” exception into Rule 60(c)(1) would displace the rule’s plain meaning and undermine finality without clear authorization. To the extent close questions remain about what is “reasonable” in particular circumstances, that inquiry can accommodate jurisdictional defects without rewriting the rule to eliminate timeliness entirely.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The text of Rule 60(c)(1) is broad and categorical: a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made “within a reasonable time,” which by its terms includes Rule 60(b)(4). This Court’s recent statement in Kemp v. United States reinforces that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)(1), and Espinosa likewise cautions that Rule 60(b)(4) “does not provide a license for litigants to sleep on their rights,” recognizing forfeiture through inaction. Reading (b)(4) as wholly exempt from any timeliness limit would undermine finality and practical workability, especially where (as here) reliance interests have accrued (e.g., near-complete administration of a bankruptcy estate). The “reasonable time” inquiry can still accommodate truly void, no-arguable-basis-for-jurisdiction cases, but it does not disappear altogether.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Rules’ text is controlling: Rule 60(c)(1) provides that a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made “within a reasonable time,” and that language naturally encompasses Rule 60(b)(4) alongside the other subsections. This Court’s instruction in United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa that Rule 60(b)(4) is limited to exceptional jurisdictional defects and “does not provide a license for litigants to sleep on their rights” supports reading (c)(1)’s timing requirement to apply even to voidness claims, preserving finality and orderly administration. Klapprott confirms only that the one-year cap for Rule 60(b)(1)–(3) does not govern (b)(4), not that (b)(4) is exempt from the separate “reasonable time” requirement in Rule 60(c)(1). While a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void, the Rules’ text and methodological consistency counsel that courts may deny a (b)(4) motion filed after an unreasonable delay under Rule 60(c)(1).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states that motions under Rule 60(b) “must be made within a reasonable time,” and its text does not carve out an exception for Rule 60(b)(4), so courts retain authority to deny relief where a party with notice sits on its rights and prejudice to reliance interests has mounted. Espinosa makes clear that “void” under Rule 60(b)(4) is narrow—reserved for exceptional jurisdictional or due-process defects—and it also contemplates that litigants can forfeit Rule 60(b)(4) arguments through inaction, which aligns with applying a reasonableness constraint. Kemp reinforces the textual point that “all” Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)(1)’s reasonable-time requirement, and the practical consequences of unlimited delay—particularly disruption to a substantially administered bankruptcy estate—counsel against treating voidness as eliminating any timeliness limitation. Procedural fairness cuts both ways: a party deprived of jurisdiction deserves a remedy, but fairness to other parties and orderly administration supports requiring prompt invocation once the defect is known.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a party may seek relief under Rule 60(b)(4) from a default judgment that is void for lack of personal jurisdiction at any time, or whether Rule 60(c)(1) requires the motion be filed within a “reasonable time.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(4) (void judgments) and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(c)(1) (timing: “must be made within a reasonable time”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void ab initio and therefore legally a nullity, so Rule 60(c)(1)’s “reasonable time” language cannot impose any deadline on a Rule 60(b)(4) motion attacking that void judgment; accordingly, courts must set aside such a judgment whenever the jurisdictional defect is raised, even long after entry.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that the Rules’ text is straightforward: Rule 60(c)(1) applies to “any motion under Rule 60(b),” including 60(b)(4), so even a void-judgment motion must be brought within a reasonable time; allowing unlimited delay would undermine finality and disrupt administration of cases (including bankruptcy estates), and the Sixth Circuit correctly treated timeliness as a constraint on 60(b)(4) relief.
key_precedents: Kemp v. United States (quoted for the proposition that all Rule 60(b) motions must be filed within a reasonable time)
United Student Aid Funds, Inc. v. Espinosa, 559 U.S. 260 (2010)
United States for Use & Benefit of Mosher Steel Co. v. Fluor Corp., 436 F.2d 383 (2d Cir. 1970)
Allstate Life Ins. Co. v. Linter Group Ltd., 994 F.2d 996 (2d Cir. 1993)
In re World Trade Ctr. Disaster Site Litig., 722 F.3d 483 (2d Cir. 2013)
Link v. Wabash R.R. Co., 370 U.S. 626 (1962)

United States v. Boch Oldsmobile, Inc., 909 F.2d 657 (1st Cir. 1990)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s due-process objection—that delay cannot “validate” a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction—is the best argument for Petitioner, but it conflates the judgment’s substantive defect with the Rules’ procedural conditions for reopening it. As Justice Kagan persuasively frames it, Rule 60(c)(1) by its terms applies to any motion “under Rule 60(b),” and recognizing a categorical (b)(4) no-deadline exception would be an atextual rewrite that undermines finality and invites strategic delay. Espinosa, emphasized by Justice Gorsuch, matters here not because it expands forfeiture, but because it confirms voidness is narrow and that Rule 60(b)(4) is not a license to “sleep on” rights—consistent with a highly forgiving, fact-specific “reasonable time” inquiry where notice and personal jurisdiction truly were absent. Kemp, as several colleagues note, reinforces the straightforward textual baseline that (c)(1)’s timing provision runs across Rule 60(b), supporting a narrow institutional holding rather than a broad constitutional carveout.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void and cannot be substantively “cured” by delay, but that framing conflates the constitutional defect with the separate question whether the Federal Rules impose procedural conditions on when a party may invoke Rule 60(b)(4) as the vehicle for relief. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Rule 60(c)(1) states categorically that a motion “under Rule 60(b)”—with no exception for (b)(4)—“must be made within a reasonable time,” and an implied carveout would rewrite the Rule atextually. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Espinosa and Kemp strengthens the textual baseline: Espinosa rejects using (b)(4) as a license to “sleep on” rights, and Kemp treats 60(c)(1) as governing Rule 60(b) motions generally, confirming that timeliness can be a procedural prerequisite without “validating” a void judgment. The due-process concern is addressed by applying “reasonable time” with maximum solicitude where the movant truly lacked notice, but the Rule’s text still forecloses a no-deadline regime.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s due-process point—no personal jurisdiction renders a judgment void—has real force, but it does not overcome the textual command in Rule 60(c)(1) that any motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be brought within a “reasonable time,” with no carveout for (b)(4). As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan persuasively frame it, enforcing a reasonable-time limit regulates access to the Rule 60 remedy; it does not “validate” an unconstitutional judgment, and the inquiry can be applied with substantial solicitude where the movant truly lacked notice. Espinosa, as Justice Gorsuch notes, confirms that 60(b)(4) is narrow and not a license to “sleep on” rights, which undercuts petitioner’s claim to an unlimited filing window; Kemp likewise supports reading 60(c)(1) as an across-the-board timing rule. I therefore see no methodological basis to create an atextual exemption that would invite strategic delay and undermine finality and reliance interests.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s textual point seriously: Rule 60(c)(1) by its terms applies to motions “under Rule 60(b),” and I understand the institutional worry—echoed by Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch—about creating an atextual carveout that invites gamesmanship. But Espinosa and Kemp, which several colleagues invoke, do not involve the core due-process failure presented by a default judgment entered without personal jurisdiction where the defendant was never properly made a party; those cases assume notice sufficient to trigger forfeiture principles, while a true jurisdictional nullity cannot be made operative by later “reasonableness” policing. In my view, applying “reasonable time” here functions not merely as a procedural condition on a remedy but as an enforcement bar that effectively insulates a void judgment against the very constitutional defect Rule 60(b)(4) exists to correct, with the predictable real-world effect of binding least-resourced defendants to judgments entered without lawful authority over them. Finality can be protected through prejudice and reliance considerations after vacatur and through other equitable tools, but it cannot justify treating a court’s lack of power over the person as something time can cure.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is constitutionally void and courts must be careful not to let procedure become a backdoor validation of a nullity. But that concern does not overcome the text and structure that Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize: Rule 60(c)(1) expressly governs any motion “under Rule 60(b)” and contains no (b)(4) carveout, so the timing requirement is best understood as a condition on accessing the reopening remedy, not a substantive cure of the jurisdictional defect. Espinosa matters here because, as Justice Gorsuch notes, it both narrows “void” and rejects treating Rule 60(b)(4) as a license to “sleep on” rights—supporting a real, though highly forgiving, reasonable-time inquiry in true no-notice/no-jurisdiction cases. Kemp reinforces the baseline textual point that (c)(1)’s timing language applies across Rule 60(b), making an atextual exemption for (b)(4) hard to justify under my pragmatic textualism.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to stress that a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is constitutionally void and cannot be “cured” by mere passage of time, but that does not answer the distinct question whether the Federal Rules may condition access to the Rule 60(b)(4) remedy on a timely motion. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Rule 60(c)(1) states without exception that a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made “within a reasonable time,” and carving out (b)(4) would effectively amend the Rule atextually—something separation-of-powers principles counsel us not to do. Espinosa reinforces that 60(b)(4) is not a license to “sleep on” rights, supporting a forgiving yet real reasonableness inquiry rather than an unlimited filing window, and Kemp further strengthens the across-the-board reading of 60(c)(1). Properly understood, applying “reasonable time” regulates the procedural vehicle for reopening; it does not retroactively “validate” a judgment that was void ab initio, and courts can apply the standard with special solicitude where notice and personal jurisdiction were truly absent.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is constitutionally void and cannot be substantively “cured” by the mere passage of time, but that does not resolve the separate question whether Rule 60’s remedial mechanism may be invoked without any temporal limit. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, Rule 60(c)(1) by its terms applies to any motion “under Rule 60(b),” and reading an unstated (b)(4) exception would be an atextual rewrite that would materially undermine finality and reliance interests. Espinosa—highlighted by Justice Gorsuch—matters because it both narrows “voidness” and explicitly warns that Rule 60(b)(4) is not a license to “sleep on” rights, which fits a forgiving-but-real “reasonable time” constraint rather than an unlimited collateral-attack regime. The institutional compromise is to apply “reasonable time” with substantial solicitude where the movant truly lacked notice/personal jurisdiction, without adopting a categorical no-deadline rule.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that a default judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void in the constitutional sense, but that does not answer the distinct textual question whether Rule 60(c)(1) imposes a procedural condition on seeking relief. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, the Rule’s language is categorical—any motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made within a reasonable time—and an atextual carveout for (b)(4) would rewrite the Rule rather than apply it. Espinosa, as Justice Gorsuch notes, reinforces that “void” is narrow and that Rule 60(b)(4) is not a license to “sleep on” rights, which coheres with a forgiving (but real) reasonableness inquiry where notice was lacking. I therefore remain with Respondent: timeliness constrains the remedy without “validating” an unconstitutional judgment, and the constitutional concern is addressed by applying “reasonable time” with special solicitude in true no-notice/no-jurisdiction cases.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that a default judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is a due-process nullity, and I share her concern that procedural doctrine not become a backdoor validation of unconstitutional process. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, Rule 60(c)(1) by its plain terms governs any motion “under Rule 60(b)” and contains no (b)(4) carveout; reading an implicit exemption would rewrite the Rule rather than apply it. Espinosa’s warning—highlighted by Justice Gorsuch—that Rule 60(b)(4) is not a license to “sleep on” rights supports treating timeliness as a condition on invoking the remedy, while making the “reasonable time” inquiry highly solicitous where the movant truly lacked notice or a meaningful opportunity to appear. Kemp further reinforces that 60(c)(1)’s timing requirement runs across Rule 60(b), so the best balance of fairness and finality is a flexible, fact-specific reasonableness standard rather than an unlimited filing window.

John Roberts.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states that “a motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time,” and that text most naturally applies to Rule 60(b)(4) as well, preserving finality and the orderly administration of judgments. While Espinosa makes clear that Rule 60(b)(4) relief is limited to the exceptional case of a truly void judgment (including certain jurisdictional defects), it does not compel a rule that such motions may be brought with no temporal constraint at all. A narrow, institutionally stabilizing approach is to hold that Rule 60(c)(1) governs but that, for genuinely void-for-lack-of-personal-jurisdiction default judgments, “reasonable time” is applied with substantial solicitude to the due process interest, rather than as a strict deadline. That reading hews closely to the Rules’ text, avoids creating a special atextual carveout, and respects the Court’s emphasis on finality and limited voidness doctrine in Espinosa.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The controlling text is Rule 60(c)(1), which provides that "[a] motion under Rule 60(b) must be made within a reasonable time," and that language on its face applies to every subsection, including Rule 60(b)(4). Petitioner’s atextual carveout would effectively amend the Rule by exempting void-judgment motions from the timing requirement, contrary to the ordinary meaning of "any motion under Rule 60(b)" and this Court’s recognition in Kemp v. United States that Rule 60(c)(1)’s timing rule governs Rule 60(b) motions. While a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void (see Espinosa’s discussion of the limited scope of Rule 60(b)(4)), the Rules may still impose procedural limits on how and when that relief is sought. Respect for the enacted Rules text and finality interests therefore supports affirming that 60(b)(4) relief must be pursued within a "reasonable time" under Rule 60(c)(1).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of Rule 60(c)(1) is categorical: a motion “under Rule 60(b)”—which necessarily includes Rule 60(b)(4)—“must be made within a reasonable time,” and we should not create an atextual carveout for voidness challenges. Espinosa confirms that “void” under Rule 60(b)(4) is a narrow category, with relief generally reserved for the exceptional case where the rendering court lacked even an arguable basis for jurisdiction, reflecting the strong federal interest in finality. Reading Rule 60(b)(4) to permit attacks “at any time” would invite strategic delay, disrupt settled expectations, and undermine the orderly administration of justice in contexts like default judgments and bankruptcy distributions. Consistent with Kemp’s recognition that Rule 60’s timing limits apply across 60(b), I would hold that even (b)(4) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)(1)’s reasonable-time requirement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A default judgment entered without personal jurisdiction offends due process and is therefore void, not merely erroneous; in that circumstance the judgment is a legal nullity and cannot be insulated by delay. Espinosa makes clear that Rule 60(b)(4) relief is reserved for exceptional cases where the rendering court lacked even an arguable basis for jurisdiction or the proceeding violated due process, and a lack of personal jurisdiction fits that core category. Although Rule 60(c)(1) states that motions under Rule 60(b) must be made within a “reasonable time,” reading that clause to bar vacatur of a truly void judgment would elevate finality over constitutional notice-and-hearing protections, especially where the defendant never had a meaningful chance to appear. The better approach is that timeliness cannot validate a judgment void for lack of personal jurisdiction, while courts retain tools to address prejudice through equitable management of the ensuing proceedings rather than by enforcing an unconstitutional judgment.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) states that a motion “under Rule 60(b)” must be made “within a reasonable time,” and that text naturally covers 60(b)(4) as well; reading an atextual no-deadline carveout for voidness would undercut the Rules’ coherence and finality interests. Espinosa instructs that 60(b)(4) relief is reserved for the exceptional case where the rendering court lacked even an arguable basis for jurisdiction, suggesting both a narrow conception of “void” and a preference against disrupting settled judgments absent extraordinary circumstances. A “reasonable time” requirement remains workable because what is reasonable can be highly forgiving when the defect is true lack of personal jurisdiction, while still preventing strategic, highly prejudicial delay. This compromise respects due-process limits on jurisdiction without turning 60(b)(4) into an unlimited, anytime collateral-attack device inconsistent with Rule 60(c)(1)’s plain language and the Court’s general insistence on administrable procedural rules (Kemp).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Rules’ text is the beginning and end: Rule 60(c)(1) says a motion “under Rule 60(b)”—without carving out (b)(4)—“must be made within a reasonable time,” so courts may enforce a timeliness constraint even when voidness is asserted. While a judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is indeed void, Rule 60(b)(4) addresses the remedy, and Rule 60(c)(1) supplies the procedural condition for invoking that remedy; reading (b)(4) to be exempt would add an atextual exception inconsistent with separation-of-powers principles governing rulemaking. Espinosa confirms that Rule 60(b)(4) “does not provide a license for litigants to sleep on their rights” and that inaction can forfeit service-based objections, reinforcing that equitable and timing limits may matter even in the void-judgment context. Kemp likewise underscores that Rule 60(b) motions are subject to Rule 60(c)(1)’s reasonable-time requirement, supporting the Sixth Circuit’s approach.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The text of Rule 60(c)(1) states that a motion under Rule 60(b) “must be made within a reasonable time,” and that clause naturally applies to “any motion under Rule 60(b),” including Rule 60(b)(4). Although a truly void judgment is limited to exceptional jurisdictional or due-process defects, Espinosa emphasizes that voidness is narrow and that parties can forfeit Rule 60(b)(4) relief through inaction, which supports a reasonable-time constraint consistent with finality and practical workability. Kemp likewise reads Rule 60(c)(1) as imposing a reasonable-time requirement across Rule 60(b) motions, and an unlimited, no-deadline rule would undermine reliance interests and orderly administration (especially where default judgments have been acted upon). Consistent with institutional concerns and judicial restraint, I would adhere to the Rules’ plain timing provision while recognizing that “reasonable time” may be generous when a judgment is truly void for lack of personal jurisdiction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of Rule 60(c)(1) is categorical: a motion “under Rule 60(b)”—which includes Rule 60(b)(4)—“must be made within a reasonable time,” and we ordinarily apply such timing provisions as written. Espinosa reinforces that Rule 60(b)(4) is not an open-ended invitation to “sleep on” rights; even where a party alleges jurisdictional infirmity, the Court has emphasized finality and limited “void” relief to exceptional cases lacking even an arguable jurisdictional basis. Reading Rule 60(b)(4) to override Rule 60(c)(1) would create atextual asymmetry within the Rule and undermine the Rules’ structural commitment to repose, while a reasonable-time standard still permits relief when the movant acts diligently upon learning of the judgment. Consistent with methodological coherence and the Rules’ plain language, timeliness is a constraint on 60(b)(4) motions, though “reasonable time” may be generous where personal jurisdiction and notice concerns are acute.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Rule 60(c)(1) by its terms applies to “any motion under Rule 60(b),” and that text naturally includes Rule 60(b)(4), so timeliness remains a procedural constraint even when the movant alleges a jurisdictional defect. Espinosa explains that Rule 60(b)(4) relief is reserved for exceptional cases and “does not provide a license for litigants to sleep on their rights,” recognizing forfeiture principles where a party had notice and failed to act, which aligns with a reasonable-time requirement. A fact-specific “reasonable time” standard also serves practical consequences and procedural fairness by protecting reliance interests and finality—especially where third parties and complex proceedings (e.g., bankruptcy estates) may be disrupted by unlimited delay. This approach leaves room to grant relief promptly where lack of personal jurisdiction truly deprived a party of due process, while preventing strategic or prejudicial late-stage collateral attacks.
